<reason>B better defended the actual requirement: individualized scrutiny rather than a human signature. It answered both pressure questions directly, supplied an auditable process standard, and acknowledged that some fraud could escape. A established a serious protective-hold argument, but repeatedly treated suspected hijacking as established theft and meaningful review as necessarily rubber-stamping. Its closing also revived the indefinite-queue comparison despite B explicitly prohibiting that outcome. B therefore provided the cleaner, more responsive case.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B’s response that withholding an existing benefit “pending review” is itself the prohibited suspension dismantled A’s comparison between a bounded hold and indefinite deprivation. Its accompanying distinction between imperfect review and nonexistent scrutiny also answered A’s claim that meaningful review was defined to exclude every failure.</best_rebuttal>
